In this rereading, I am struck by the state’s control of women’s bodies, the oppression of the masses, the fates of people of color, and the erasure of language. I think of the many dystopian novels that have been published since 1984, novels such as Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler, Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro, The Road by Cormac McCarthy, or The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood. Each of these writers offers a critique of society that has a powerful pull not only on our imaginations, but also on our sense of self. Who are we and what are the implications of our actions? Because of its ability to hold both story and ideas in the palm of its hand, 1984 was a joyful reread for me, even with its imperfections. In this rereading. I considered the book’s larger intentions while also asking a basic question: Is it a good story? I tried to recapture the wonder of a child encountering Orwell for the first time, and in that, I probably failed. It is impossible to do so when I no longer possess the innocence of youth. I am now more firmly grounded in reading history and in a set of expectations. Now. when I pick up a book, I bring my own story to it. Furthermore, the book is too imprinted in our collective consciousness, too many of its references used in other contexts. Big Brother. Ministry of Truth. Two plus two equals five. Thought Police. Newspeak. Orwell’s ideas have permeated popular culture. This book has pushed me to think about love and community as healing forces, as powerful modes of resistance. Although the nature of dystopian novels is that they do not typically embrace such optimism. I tend to agree with Margaret Atwood’s observation that because the coda at the end of the book is written in the past tense, it suggests that the government does not win. If the government does not ultimately win, that means the people are more powerful than we know. I am back to the wonder of discovering Animal Farm, back to rejoicing at the power of literature to weave a spell and craft a vision at the same time. Somehow I have managed to discover a way to enter 1984 seventy-five years after its initial publication and find new appreciation for it, new love for it. Yes. I have said it. I loved so much about this book, and I understand its lasting impact. So I suppose, in the end, I have succeeded in recapturing that initial thrill of discovering the possibilities of literature. —Dolen Perkins-Valdez FOREWORD George Orwell was bom Eric Arthur Blair on June 25, 1903, in Motihari, a small town in Bengal near the Nepalese border, and in the middle of a highly productive opium district. His father was there working as an agent for the British Opium Department, not arresting growers, but supervising quality control of the product, in which Britain had long enjoyed a monopoly. A year later, young Eric was back in England with his mother and sister, and did not return to the region until 1922, as a junior officer of the Indian Imperial Police, in Burma. That job paid well, but when he came home on leave in 1927, much to the distress of his father, he decided to chuck it, because what he really wanted to do with his life was be a writer, and that is what he became. In 1933, with the publication of his first book, Down and Out in Paris and London, he adopted the pseudonym of George Orwell, which was the name he was known by from then on. Orwell was one of the names he had used while tramping round England, and may have been suggested by a river of the same name in Suffolk. 1984 was Orwell’s last book—by the time it came out, in 1949, he had published twelve others, including the highly acclaimed and popular Animal Farm. In an essay from the summer of 1946, “Why I Write,” he recalled, “Animal Farm was the first book in which I tried, with full consciousness of what I was doing, to fuse political purpose and artistic purpose into one whole. I have not written a novel for seven years, but I hope to write another fairly soon. It is bound to be a failure, every book is a failure, but I know with some clarity what kind of book I want to write.” Shortly after this, he was at work on 1984. In a way, this novel has been a victim of the success of Animal Farm, which most people were content to read as a straightforward allegory about the melancholy fate of the Russian revolution. From the minute Big Brother’s mustache makes its appearance in the second paragraph of 1984, many readers, thinking right away of Stalin, have tended to carry over the habit of point-for-point analogy from the earlier work. Although Big Brother’s face certainly is Stalin’s, just as the despised Party heretic Emmanuel Goldstein’s face is Trotsky’s, the two do not quite line up with their models as neatly as Napoleon and Snowball did in Animal Farm. This did not keep the book from being marketed in the United States as a sort of anticommunist tract. It arrived in the thick of the McCarthy era, when “Communism” was damned officially as a monolithic, worldwide menace, and there was no point in even distinguishing between Stalin and Trotsky, any more than for shepherds to be instructing sheep in the nuances of wolf recognition.
